Context/Background: ASXL1 plays key roles in epigenetic regulation of early developmental gene expression. De novo protein-truncating mutations in ASXL1 cause Bohring-Opitz syndrome (BOS), a rare neurodevelopmental condition characterized by severe intellectual disabilities, distinctive facial features, hypertrichosis, increased risk of Wilms tumor, and variable congenital anomalies, including heart defects and severe skeletal defects giving rise to a typical BOS posture. These BOS-causing ASXL1 variants are also high-prevalence somatic driver mutations in acute myeloid leukemia.  We used primary cells from individuals with BOS (n = 18) and controls (n = 49) to dissect gene regulatory changes caused by ASXL1 mutations using comprehensive multiomics assays for chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), DNA methylation, histone methylation binding, and transcriptome in peripheral blood and skin fibroblasts.
Prompt: Based on the results of the blood and fibroblast transcriptomic DEG analyses of BOS vs controls, provide a discussion of the common and distinct pathways found between blood and fibroblast and any relevance to the presence in the BOS samples of ASXL1 truncating mutations.
output_text:
Introduction/Context  
Bohring-Opitz syndrome (BOS) is caused by de novo protein-truncating mutations in ASXL1, a chromatin regulator that shapes developmental gene expression. Here, transcriptomes of primary skin fibroblasts (n = 18 BOS, 49 controls) and peripheral blood (same individuals) were profiled by RNA-seq. Differential expression analysis (DESeq2) identified 999 significant genes (padj < 0.05) in fibroblasts (e.g., UGT3A2, TNMD, CNTN4) and 2 118 in blood (e.g., SLC7A3, GRIK5, VANGL2). GSEA (pre-ranked by log2FoldChange) then revealed tissue-specific and shared pathways. For details, see jciinsight-8-167744 sdt1-26 Tables S11 (Fibro-DEG) and S12 (Blood-DEG).

Keywords  
• ASXL1 truncation  
• Epigenetic regulation  
• Neurodevelopment/axonogenesis  
• Innate immune response  
• Tissue specificity

Balanced Analysis  
Both cell types share a coordinated down-regulation of innate immune- and cytokine-related modules (Reactome “Immune System,” KEGG “Phagosome,” MSigDB “Inflammatory Response”), suggesting that ASXL1 truncations disrupt normal blood-lineage immune programs and immune-related gene expression in fibroblasts. In fibroblasts only, strong up-regulation of neuronal development pathways (axonogenesis/axon guidance) points to de-repression of neurodevelopmental gene networks, consistent with ASXL1’s role in modulating early developmental chromatin states. Blood uniquely exhibits robust suppression of multiple infection-response pathways (tuberculosis, Staphylococcus aureus, Leishmaniasis) and chemokine/IL-6 signaling, whereas fibroblasts show minimal microbial-response enrichment beyond a single down-regulated oxygen response pathway. Reactome “Scavenging of Heme” is up in blood but absent in fibroblasts, reflecting tissue-specific compensation for altered erythrocyte turnover or inflammation.  

Targeted (keyword-guided) subset  
Filtering the fibroblast GSEA results for CNTN4/VANGL2/GRIK5/GREM2 highlighted that CNTN4 leads multiple axon-related terms, while GREM2 contributes to the oxygen-response pathway. In blood, IL1B and TLR2 feature prominently in inflammatory and pattern-recognition pathways, underscoring disrupted innate immunity.  

Key Genes/Proteins (leading edge)  
Up  
| Gene   | Direction | Role/Function                      | Pathway(s)                   |
|--------|-----------|------------------------------------|------------------------------|
| CNTN4  | Up        | Neuronal adhesion/contactin family | Axonogenesis, Axon Guidance |
| VANGL2 | Up        | Planar cell polarity               | — (Juxtaposed in both)      |
| S100B  | Up        | Calcium-binding in glia            | Nervous System Development  |
| IGKV1-16… | Up     | Immunoglobulin light chains        | Scavenging of Heme          |

Down  
| Gene    | Direction | Role/Function                  | Pathway(s)                     |
|---------|-----------|--------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| IL1B    | Down      | Pro-inflammatory cytokine      | Inflammatory Response, KEGG    |
| TLR2    | Down      | Pattern recognition receptor   | Phagosome, KEGG pathways       |
| SIRPA   | Down      | Inhibitory immune receptor     | Immune System (both)           |
| MEFV    | Down      | Inflammasome component         | Hallmark Inflammatory Response |

Shared leading-edge genes (e.g., IL1B, TLR2, SIRPA) occur in blood and fibroblast immune-related terms, supporting a core ASXL1-mediated immune dysregulation across tissues. Neuronal/upregulated genes (CNTN4) are fibroblast-specific.  

Comparisons  
• Common: suppression of innate immunity and cytokine signaling (higher confidence).  
• Fibroblast-specific: activation of neurodevelopmental/axon pathways.  
• Blood-specific: broad down-regulation of infection-response KEGG modules; compensatory up in heme clearance.  

Implications  
ASXL1 truncation likely impairs PRC2-mediated silencing, leading to ectopic activation of developmental programs in somatic cells (e.g., CNTN4) and dampened immune-response gene networks. In blood, immune suppression may contribute to leukemia susceptibility, whereas in fibroblasts, activation of neurogenic pathways may underlie BOS neurodevelopmental defects.  

Next Steps & Clarification  
1. Validate whether Wnt signaling networks (not detected by GSEA here) are misregulated at the transcript level in fibroblasts.  
2. Assess chromatin marks (H3K27me3/H2AK119Ub) at leading-edge immune genes (IL1B, TLR2) in blood vs fibroblasts.  
3. Investigate whether up-regulation of axonogenesis genes in fibroblasts reflects direct ASXL1 targets or compensation via other Polycomb proteins.  
4. Examine functional consequences of suppressed phagosome and cytokine pathways in patient-derived immune cells (e.g., monocytes).
